A Beach Worth Saving

When our school announced a volunteer clean-up of a beach on the Caspian coast, only a few students signed up. Most of us thought it would be a boring way to spend a Sunday. I went mainly because my best friend, Rashad, had promised to bring his camera.

What we found surprised everyone. In just three hours, thirty volunteers collected more than two hundred bags of rubbish. Plastic bottles were the most common item, but we also found fishing nets, shoes, a broken chair and thousands of tiny pieces of plastic mixed with the sand. A biologist from a local environmental group explained that these small pieces are especially dangerous, because birds and fish often mistake them for food.

Rashad's photos turned out to be the most powerful part of the day. He posted a 'before and after' picture of the beach, and within a week it had been shared hundreds of times. People we had never met wrote to ask when the next clean-up would take place.

The next event attracted almost a hundred volunteers, including several families with small children. Looking back, I realise that the beach did not change because of one Sunday. It changed because people saw what was possible and decided to act. Cleaning the beach is useful, but the real goal, the biologist reminded us, is to stop the rubbish from getting there in the first place.

because he needed points for school
because his friend was going to bring a camera
because he wanted to meet a biologist

quizzes.passage:
How Habits Work

Why is it so easy to check your phone and so hard to start your homework? According to some researchers, the answer lies in the way habits are formed. They describe every habit as a loop made of three parts: a cue, a routine and a reward.

The cue is the signal that starts the behaviour — for example, the sound of a notification. The routine is the behaviour itself: picking up the phone and scrolling. The reward is the pleasant feeling that follows, such as seeing a funny message. When this loop is repeated many times, the brain begins to connect the cue with the reward, and the routine becomes almost automatic.

The good news is that the same loop can be used to build useful habits. Experts suggest keeping the cue simple and visible: if you want to read more, leave a book on your pillow. They also recommend starting with a very small routine, such as reading just two pages, so that it does not feel like hard work. Finally, giving yourself a small reward, like ticking a box on a calendar, helps the brain remember that the behaviour is worth repeating.

Breaking a bad habit is usually harder than starting a new one. Instead of simply trying to stop, it often works better to keep the same cue and reward but change the routine. A student who snacks when bored, for instance, might go for a short walk instead.

Dear Leyla,

It has been almost three months since I arrived in Germany for my exchange year, and I finally have time to write a proper letter. The first weeks were much harder than I expected. I had studied German for two years, but on my first day at school I understood almost nothing. Everyone spoke so fast! I went home and cried, and I seriously thought about coming back.

My host family helped me more than I can say. Every evening at dinner, my host mother asked me to describe my day in German, and she never laughed at my mistakes. My host brother, Jonas, introduced me to his friends and took me to his football club, even though I am a terrible player.

Now things are different. Last week I gave a short presentation about Azerbaijan in my geography class. I showed photos of Baku and the mountains of Quba, and my classmates asked so many questions that the teacher had to stop us. I have also learned to cook a German potato salad, although I still prefer our plov.

The most important thing I have learned is that feeling lost is normal at the beginning. If you decide to apply for the exchange programme next year, don't let the first difficult weeks scare you. Write back soon and tell me everything about school!

With love,
Sabina
